title: JWT posture of the ~202 edge functions — MEASURED (13 gated), and WHY os_* are edge-open
content: MEASURED 2 Sep 2026 from the live project and supabase/config.toml (regenerated to match). EXACTLY 13 functions are verify_jwt=true at the edge: brand_upload, contact_submit, customer_intelligence, negotiation_assistant, procurement_api, project_api, put_src, quote_quality, rate_dims, src_io, stripe_setup, wa_optin_set, wa_templates_watch. All 7 os_* admin functions are verify_jwt=FALSE at the edge — this is BY DESIGN, not a gap: they share the build-mode open door (see the "Build-mode OPEN DOOR" record / fn_os_open_access), and verify_jwt=true would sever it. Off the build-mode path they are guarded IN CODE (admin.auth.getUser + app_secrets.admin_emails). config.toml is a generated MIRROR of the live values (scripts/gen_supabase_config.mjs); its header had been hand-edited to falsely claim 20 including os_* — corrected by regeneration. RULE for an agent: config.toml is generated from live; never hand-edit it, and never trust its header over the count of per-function verify_jwt=true blocks (13). Edge-gating os_* is only correct AFTER build mode is retired (a launch decision). Every other (~180) function is verify_jwt=false by design: internal/shared-secret (requireInternal/fn_internal_auth) or in-code guarded.
source: MEASURED vs live project + supabase/config.toml regenerated 2 Sep 2026; build-mode door is why os_* are edge-open

title: Server-to-server auth: requireInternal / fn_internal_auth and the legacy shared __secret
content: Most internal functions are invoked by crons, the kernel, or sibling functions, not browsers. Two mechanisms authenticate those hops. NEW: _shared/internal_auth.ts requireInternal(admin, body.__secret, fnName) calls DB fn_internal_auth, which checks the presented credential against a per-context row scoped to fnName; scope, rotation and attribution live in the database, not in 137 copies of a string compare. It FAILS CLOSED — if the verifier is unreachable the call is refused (503). ~130 functions import it (agent_*, kb_*, ai_gateway, send_*, refunds_api, wa_inbound, qa_mint, etc.). LEGACY: fn_internal_auth still accepts the ONE shared secret app_secrets.inbound_secret (registered as a legacy credential with scope '*'), so moving a function to the module changed nothing about who can call it — it only started recording which credential did. That single string once authenticated 43 cron jobs, 42 functions and 20 DB functions; one disclosure is total and it cannot be scoped or rotated without changing every caller at once. Attack implications: (1) the shared secret is the crown-jewel; leaking it grants internal-caller identity across the estate. (2) requireInternal deliberately does NOT distinguish out_of_scope from unknown_credential in its 403, to avoid a scope-discovery oracle. (3) The declaredCaller (e.g. ai_gateway's body.fn) is recorded as an unverified CLAIM, never as authorization.
source: supabase/functions/_shared/internal_auth.ts; ~130 functions grep-match requireInternal; refunds_api/qa_mint/ai_gateway import it

title: Retired 410 surfaces — dead auth-bypass and takeover primitives deliberately removed
content: Eleven functions are permanently disabled and return HTTP 410 with a self-naming body: auth_api, dev_login, qa_login, brand_upload, kb_retrieve, licence_reminder, orchestrate, src_io, support_ai, voice_otp, voice_otp_capture. The security-critical retirements: auth_api (27 Jul 2026) was unauthenticated and its signup_customer/signup_supplier path minted a CONFIRMED auth user with a caller-chosen password for any email lacking an auth user — account SQUATTING of prospects/competitors, arriving pre-verified (email_confirm:true); replaced by login_otp + kyc. dev_login and qa_login were QA sign-in shortcuts (session/account minters) with no place in production. The 410 body names the function and its replacement on purpose: a bare {"error":"disabled"} taught callers nothing AND, being 8 chars, gave deploy-parity no distinctive literal so the function reported UNVERIFIED. For a security agent: a request that still hits these should be treated as recon against known-removed weaknesses; the live sign-in path is login_otp (passwordless codes) and account completion is kyc. Do not revive any of these — the comments explicitly forbid it.
source: grep 'status: 410' across functions/ (11 hits); auth_api/index.ts and dev_login/index.ts and qa_login/index.ts header comments

title: Stripe payment surface: stripe_webhook, stripe_checkout, stripe_confirm, stripe_setup
content: The reveal-fee money path. stripe_webhook (verify_jwt=false, must be public for Stripe): verifies the Stripe-Signature HMAC-SHA256 itself over t.payload using app_secrets.stripe_webhook_secret, with a 600s timestamp tolerance as a replay guard and a constant-time compare. It accepts TWO signing secrets — live (stripe_webhook_secret) then test (stripe_webhook_secret_test) — tried in full, so a test-mode delivery can never be validated by the live secret; rejects with 400 before parsing on bad signature. Every exit writes agent_runs. stripe_checkout (verify_jwt=false but enforces its own auth): Bearer JWT -> admin.auth.getUser -> customers row, then an OWNERSHIP check that the quote's inquiry.customer_id == this customer before creating a Checkout Session; return_url host is allowlisted (quotesdone.com/www/*.vercel.app) after a 27 Jul open-redirect fix that had let a crafted return_url exfiltrate the session id. stripe_setup is the only Stripe fn pinned verify_jwt=true. Abuse surface: the webhook is the settlement authority — if a signing secret leaked, forged checkout.session.completed events could mark reveals paid without money; the dual-secret + tolerance + constant-time compare are the defenses. stripe_checkout's IDOR guard (inq.customer_id !== cust.id -> 403) is what stops one buyer paying to reveal on another's inquiry.
source: supabase/functions/stripe_webhook/index.ts (verifySig, TOLERANCE_SECONDS=600, dual secret); stripe_checkout/index.ts (getUser+ownership, safeBase allowlist)

title: Refund surface: refunds_api (founder/admin) and refund_flow (customer) — real money out
content: refunds_api (verify_jwt=false) is the founder's refund console. Auth is dual: body.__secret via requireInternal OR an admin-email JWT (admin.auth.getUser then membership in app_secrets.admin_emails, lowercased). Actions: list_pending, list_recent, resolve{transaction_id, decision, note}. Since v5 (27 Jul 2026) approve ACTUALLY calls Stripe's /v1/refunds with Idempotency-Key = transaction id (so a double-click cannot refund twice), and writes refund_status='refunded' ONLY after Stripe confirms — fail closed. That status flip triggers supplier_dues, matching_blocked and the collections_legal ladder, so a spurious approve costs a customer money, a supplier standing, and a chargeback; on Stripe failure NOTHING changes. Failures also raise founder_alerts + notifications out-of-band so they reach a human even if the admin UI ignores the response. refund_flow (verify_jwt=false) is the CUSTOMER side of the unresponsive-supplier ladder: Bearer JWT -> getUser -> customers row (auth replicated from customer_api), actions list/state/notify. Timing (1 working day to notify, 3 to founder call) lives in Postgres fn_refund_state/fn_notify_supplier honouring Asia/Dubai holidays. GOVERNANCE: every refund of any amount requires the founder (his 17 Aug 2026 ruling); refund_flow can start the ladder but cannot approve — approval is refunds_api under admin identity only.
source: supabase/functions/refunds_api/index.ts (authed(): __secret|admin JWT, stripeRefund idempotency); refund_flow/index.ts (customer JWT auth header)

title: os_api — the OS/admin backend: JWT owner/admin, read-only preview key, verified-founder gate
content: os_api (verify_jwt=false, but self-gated) is the backend for QuotesDone OS, the internal command centre — the highest-value single endpoint. Auth: Bearer JWT -> admin.auth.getUser -> isAdmin(email), which passes if fn_role_of returns owner/admin OR the email is in app_secrets.admin_emails. It routes ~24 workspace RPCs (ws.exec, ws.finance, ws.fraud, ws.refunds, ws.governance, ws.founder_queue, ...) and dozens of actions. Two independent gates classify every action: an ActionClass table (read_only|mutating|mode_control|founder_gated, no default — the build fails if a dispatched action is unclassified) and DB Observe/Control mode (control_mode_action). A READ-ONLY PREVIEW bypass exists via header x-os-key: it can reach read_only actions only; mutating/founder_gated actions are unreachable by the preview key (a 15 Aug fix — the old gate wrongly treated 'unregistered' as 'read-only'). PCCR-003 (21 Aug 2026): founder identity is now a VERIFIED auth subject — asCaller() rebuilds a PostgREST client carrying the request's bearer token so fn_phase_c_require_founder resolves the subject the project's JWT secret verified, not a caller-supplied email string (which service_role could previously spoof). Abuse surface: compromise of an admin_emails mailbox or the x-os-key grants OS access; the classification table is what keeps the preview key from writing.
source: supabase/functions/os_api/index.ts (isAdmin, asCaller/ANON client, ACTION_CLASS table, WS map, x-os-key CORS header)

title: ai_gateway — the single inference router and its abuse/spend surface
content: ai_gateway (verify_jwt=false) is THE one place every model call should pass; before it, ~68 functions called OpenRouter directly (37 with hand-rolled fetch, invisible to cost logs). Auth: requireInternal(admin, body.__secret, 'ai_gateway') — internal callers present __secret and declare body.fn (an unverified claim used only for routing/attribution). Order of operations is cheapest-first: (1) rate limit (rate_key gives per-caller/per-sender ceilings, e.g. wa_inbound 20/hr), (2) Level-0 templates+FAQ with NO model, (3) fn_ai_route picks tier by calling fn/task_class and substitutes for capability from the payload's modalities (vision/audio/web/tools), (4) tier='none' declines, (5) budget halt per department, (6) exact then SEMANTIC cache on free in-region embeddings, (7) the call with Anthropic prompt caching + hard token cap + model ladder, (8) log real cost. It imports paidProviderGate (kernel K12) so no paid provider is reached without explicit allow. dry_run:true runs 1-6 without spending. Abuse surface: as a public endpoint holding provider keys, its guards against unbounded third-party spend are the __secret gate + the rate limiter + the budget halt + K12; a leaked internal secret turns it into a metered but attacker-driven spend and jailbreak funnel, which is why rate limiting is step 1 before any spend.
source: supabase/functions/ai_gateway/index.ts (header order-of-operations, imports requireInternal + paidProviderGate); _shared/paid_gate.ts

title: OTP sign-in (login_otp/mobile_otp) and the qa_mint account-creation primitive
content: login_otp (verify_jwt=false) is the live passwordless sign-in. 6-digit codes are stored as HMAC-SHA256(code, app_secrets.otp_hmac_key), never a bare SHA-256 (a million-entry rainbow table would reverse an unsalted hash from one table leak); it FAILS CLOSED if otp_hmac_key is missing. Guess-rate is capped: EMAIL_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=5 per issued code and EMAIL_VERIFY_PER_IP_HOUR=30. The email branch consults email_suppressions before sending (fails OPEN on lookup error so a suppression outage cannot lock everyone out). The SMS branch adds a per-CALLER cap and an absolute hourly ceiling on the signup path (19 Jul 2026) to stop an attacker walking UAE mobile numbers to trigger billable Twilio SMS at 6/number/hr with no global ceiling — both unbounded spend and SMS harassment sent in our name. qa_mint (verify_jwt=false) is a STANDING account-creation primitive: it calls admin.auth.admin.createUser(email_confirm:true) for an arbitrary email. Two guards: requireInternal(__secret) AND app_secrets.qa_mint_enabled must equal 'true' (kept OFF in production; M13). A 27 Jul fail-closed fix requires the stored secret be >=24 real chars so a caller posting {} can no longer match an empty secret and gain service-role account minting. Abuse surface: qa_mint enabled + secret leak = arbitrary confirmed-account creation.
source: supabase/functions/login_otp/index.ts (otpHash HMAC, attempt caps, isSuppressed, SMS abuse control); qa_mint/index.ts (requireInternal + qa_mint_enabled + secretOk>=24)

title: Inbound webhook surface: wa_inbound (Twilio), resend_webhook (Resend), inbound_email
content: Webhooks are public by necessity (verify_jwt=false) and each proves origin differently. wa_inbound (Twilio WhatsApp on +1 218 316 6814) had NO auth token stored, so classic X-Twilio-Signature HMAC-SHA1 is impossible; instead it verifies PROVENANCE by calling Twilio's REST API to confirm the payload's MessageSid is a real inbound message from the claimed sender (v10, 19 Jul 2026). This closed an OPEN RELAY: previously anyone POSTing From/Body made the function run an LLM completion and sendWa(From,...) — message-bombing any number from our business line plus unbounded Twilio/OpenRouter spend. It also imports requireInternal and routes replies through ai_gateway with rate_key (20 msgs/hr/sender). resend_webhook verifies the Svix signature (svix-id/timestamp/signature) with app_secrets.resend_webhook_signing_secret AND keeps a ?key= query secret as a second factor (v4, 19 Jul 2026 — v3's query-secret-only was weak: the URL leaks via dashboard, history, referrers, proxy logs, letting forged bounce/complaint events add arbitrary addresses to email_suppressions, silently blacklisting real users). inbound_email/resend_inbound ingest email (x-webhook-secret header / __secret) and create leads/inquiries. Attack lens: any webhook whose origin proof is weak becomes a spoofable write into leads, suppressions, or the messaging relay.
source: supabase/functions/wa_inbound/index.ts (PROVENANCE block, REST lookup); resend_webhook/index.ts (Svix + ?key= second factor); inbound_email/index.ts CORS x-webhook-secret

title: Customer portal surface: customer_api, customer_portal, customer_documents, reveal_invoice, project_api
content: The buyer-facing functions share one auth shape and one tenant boundary. Each does Bearer JWT -> admin.auth.getUser -> match a customers row (by user.id then email fallback), returning 401 if no user and 403/400 if no customer profile. Because every function runs as SERVICE_ROLE (RLS is bypassed), the ONLY thing scoping a buyer to their own data is an explicit in-code ownership check. Examples that must hold on every data path: stripe_checkout and reveal_invoice compare tx.customer_id !== cust.id -> 403 'Not your transaction'; customer_api.my_inquiries filters by cust.id. This is the primary IDOR surface — any customer action that takes a quote_id/inquiry_id/transaction_id and forgets the customer_id equality check would let one authenticated buyer read another's quotes, drawings (signed URLs to quote-files/drawing-files/agent-docs buckets), or invoices. customer_api also rate-limits (INQUIRY_LIMIT_PER_HOUR=20, PDF_LIMIT_PER_HOUR=40) and sanitizes uploads via _shared/attachment.ts (SAFE_UPLOAD+SAFE_CAD, 25MB cap). project_api is one of the 20 verify_jwt=true functions. customer_intelligence (verify_jwt=true) is admin analytics, not a buyer surface. Review priority: grep each buyer action for the customer_id/cust.id ownership predicate before it returns rows or a signed URL.
source: supabase/functions/customer_portal/index.ts and reveal_invoice/index.ts (getUser+customers row, tx.customer_id!==cust.id 403); customer_api/index.ts (limits, sanitizeUpload)

title: Supplier surface: supplier_api/supplier_portal/supplier_onboard and quote-anonymity enforcement
content: Supplier functions (supplier_api, supplier_portal, supplier_onboard, supplier_ack, supplier_review, supplier_pay, supplier_catalog_ingest; all verify_jwt=false) authenticate suppliers by JWT->getUser->leads row, with __secret for internal calls. Two security-material behaviors beyond auth. (1) COMMISSION-PROTECTING ANONYMITY: submit_quote runs scrubIdentity over the supplier's typed scope/conditions/exclusions/notes BEFORE the buyer can see them pre-reveal. The FORM path was previously served verbatim (only the upload path was scrubbed by quote_extract's model), so a supplier typing 'call Ahmed on 050..., Al Noor Trading LLC, alnoor.ae' handed the buyer everything the 3% reveal fee is charged for, cutting the platform out (27 Jul 2026 fix). scrubIdentity redacts, case-insensitively, the supplier's own company name (with LLC/FZE/Trading/Contracting suffix variants), emails, URLs, bare .ae/.com domains, and UAE phone formats (+971/00971/0+8-9 digits), collecting originals into quotes.masked_terms; it deliberately over-redacts. (2) TERMS-ACCEPTANCE EVIDENCE: registration records accepted_terms_at, _version AND originating IP (x-forwarded-for/cf-connecting-ip/x-real-ip), because the 3% non-response fine drives an automated collections->legal path and a disputed fine must evidence THIS party accepted THAT version at THAT time from THAT address (19 Jul 2026 fix). Attack lens: any quote-return path that skips scrubIdentity leaks supplier identity and voids the commission.
source: supabase/functions/supplier_api/index.ts (scrubIdentity, ID_PATTERNS, companyRe, clientIp evidence block)

title: Kernel K12 paid-provider gate (_shared/paid_gate.ts) — fail-closed inference authorization
content: paidProviderGate(admin, model) in _shared/paid_gate.ts is the single client-side authority every function that can reach a paid inference provider must consult; it calls DB fn_kernel_paid_provider_gate and treats ANYTHING other than an explicit allowed===true as DENIED. It exists because the pattern it replaced had three routes to an unauthorized paid call: the RPC throws and a catch falls through to push the model; the RPC returns null and `pf &&` short-circuits; the RPC returns a shape without `allowed` and a strict `=== false` misses it. The rewrite makes refusal the default and permission the special case — there is NO catch that continues: a throw -> DENY('gate_unreachable'), null/undefined -> DENY('gate_returned_nothing','absence is not permission'), non-object -> DENY('gate_malformed'), missing/non-boolean allowed -> denial. assertPaidProviderAllowed throws PaidProviderDenied so a refusal reaches logs as a decision, not a mystery. Security relevance: this is the spend-control chokepoint; combined with ai_gateway's budget halt and the OpenRouter hold, it is what prevents a compromised or buggy caller from running up provider bills. A security agent auditing a new inference path should confirm it routes through ai_gateway (which imports this) rather than calling a provider directly and bypassing K12.
source: supabase/functions/_shared/paid_gate.ts (DENY helper, paidProviderGate strict allowed===true, assertPaidProviderAllowed)

title: Structural posture: every function runs service_role behind wildcard CORS — in-code guard is the only boundary
content: Two facts shape the whole surface. (1) SERVICE_ROLE EVERYWHERE: ~191 of the functions construct their Supabase client with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, so RLS is bypassed on every query the function makes. There is therefore NO database-level tenant isolation on the edge tier — the customers/leads/admin_emails ownership check written in TypeScript is the entire authorization boundary. A missing or fail-open check is a full cross-tenant read/write, not a partial one. (2) WILDCARD CORS: functions set Access-Control-Allow-Origin:'*' with Allow-Headers 'authorization, content-type' (plus x-os-key on os_api, x-webhook-secret on inbound_email). Any web origin can invoke them; browser same-origin policy provides no protection, so every guard must be server-side. Practical review method for this estate: for any function, answer three questions in order — is it verify_jwt true or false (config.toml)? what in-code gate does it apply (requireInternal/__secret, getUser+row, admin_emails, or none)? and for every action that returns rows or takes a write, is there an ownership/role predicate the caller cannot forge? The functions holding secrets and running as service_role with only a shared __secret between them and the world (ai_gateway, send_*, kb_*, agent_*) are where a single leaked inbound_secret does the most damage.
source: grep SERVICE_ROLE across functions/ (191 index.ts hits); CORS object in customer_api/os_api/inbound_email; config.toml for verify_jwt

title: Bulk data-egress and privacy functions: export_* knowledge/leads and pdpl_erase/retention_purge
content: Two clusters move or destroy data in bulk and warrant separate scrutiny. EGRESS: export_all_knowledge, export_cat_knowledge and export_leads_csv (all verify_jwt=false, all gated by requireInternal/__secret) can return the company's entire knowledge corpus or the leads/supplier list — a mass-exfiltration primitive if the internal credential leaks, and export_leads_csv in particular emits PII (contact names, emails, phones) of suppliers/buyers. They are internal-only by design; there is no buyer/supplier JWT path to them, so the only defense is the shared/scoped secret and they should be high on any credential-leak blast-radius list. DESTRUCTION: pdpl_erase and pdpl_request implement UAE PDPL data-subject erasure, and retention_purge enforces retention windows — these are the deletion authorities. Because a delete is irreversible and cross-table (e.g. documents feeds doc_backups which retries), an erroneously-triggered or spoofed call is data loss, so like all internal writers they require requireInternal and should fail closed. Attack lens: an attacker with the internal secret could either exfiltrate (export_*) or destroy (pdpl_erase/retention_purge); both are reasons the legacy shared inbound_secret must be retired in favour of per-context credentials, since a scoped credential for one context cannot reach these.
source: supabase/functions/export_*/index.ts and pdpl_erase/pdpl_request/retention_purge (requireInternal callers; verify_jwt=false in config.toml)

title: The real data boundary is edge-function code, not RLS: service_role bypasses everything
content: QuotesDone's primary data path is NOT PostgREST-with-RLS. The Next.js frontend makes ~0 direct .rpc()/table calls; instead 190 of 202 Deno edge functions instantiate their client with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY (396 grep hits across supabase/functions/*/index.ts, e.g. portal/index.ts: `const admin = createClient(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY)`). service_role has rolbypassrls=true, so every one of those functions reads/writes freely and RLS is never consulted on that path. Consequence for engineers and security agents: for the main app, database RLS is defense-in-depth, not the enforcement point. The actual authorization gate for a given request is the application logic inside the edge function (JWT verification, role_guard checks, ownership joins) BEFORE it touches the DB with the service key. Two hard implications: (1) a leaked SERVICE_ROLE_KEY defeats all RLS at once — protect it like a root password; RLS gives you nothing against it. (2) When reviewing an access-control bug, read the edge function's own auth code first; the RLS policy on the table is usually irrelevant because the caller is service_role. The narrow PostgREST-direct surface (anon/authenticated JWT hitting tables/RPCs) is a small secondary door, covered separately.
source: supabase/functions/portal/index.ts and 190 edge functions grepped for SERVICE_ROLE_KEY; pg_roles.rolbypassrls for service_role; memory 'a mention is not a call' (frontend has 0 .rpc()).

title: RLS posture: 605 public tables, all RLS-enabled, 588 deny-all with zero policies
content: Every base table in the public schema (605 of 605, relkind='r') has relrowsecurity=true; zero tables have RLS disabled. Of these, 588 have NO policy at all and 17 carry policies (17 policy rows total). An RLS-enabled table with no policy is deny-all to any role that does not bypass RLS: anon and authenticated (rolbypassrls=false) get zero rows regardless of grants. service_role and postgres (rolbypassrls=true) ignore RLS entirely and still read everything. The Supabase security advisor reports 638 `rls_enabled_no_policy` INFO lints — this is the INTENDED architecture here, not a backlog of defects. The design is: lock every table at the row layer, expose nothing to PostgREST by default, and mediate all real access through service_role edge functions or a handful of SECURITY DEFINER RPCs. When you add a new table it inherits this stance only if you (a) enable RLS and (b) add no anon/authenticated policy — verify both, because a new table without RLS enabled would be readable by anyone the moment a grant exists. Do not 'fix' the 638 no-policy lints by adding permissive policies; that would open tables the model deliberately keeps shut.
source: pg_class.relrowsecurity over public schema (605 tables, 0 disabled); pg_policies count (17 policies on 17 tables); get_advisors(security) = 638 rls_enabled_no_policy lints.

title: GRANT is evaluated before RLS — a policy without a table grant is dead code
content: Postgres checks the table-level privilege (GRANT) BEFORE any RLS policy runs. If a role lacks SELECT on the table, it gets 'permission denied for table' and the policy is never reached. This trips people up in this database: 13 tables carry an `os_owner_admin_read` policy for the authenticated role (customers, inquiries, transactions, ai_cost_log, expenses, gl_journal, kb_chunks, leads, org_agents, risk_register, vision_horizon, workflow, edge_health_probe) whose USING clause is `fn_role_of(auth.jwt()->>'email') = ANY(ARRAY['owner','admin'])`. But has_table_privilege('authenticated', <tbl>, 'SELECT') is FALSE for all 13 — authenticated holds no SELECT grant — so none of those policies can ever be exercised via PostgREST. brand_assets has a `brand_assets_public_read USING(true)` policy for anon+authenticated, yet neither role has the grant, so it too is inert. These policies are harmless (they fail closed via the missing grant) but misleading: reading pg_policies alone overstates the exposed surface. Rule for auditing this DB: a table is reachable by a PostgREST role only if BOTH has_table_privilege(role,tbl,'SELECT')=true AND a permissive policy matches. Check the grant first. The founder OS dashboard reads customers/inquiries/transactions through SECURITY DEFINER RPCs (running as postgres), not through these authenticated policies.
source: has_table_privilege() checks on the 13 os_owner_admin_read tables + brand_assets (all authenticated/anon SELECT = false); pg_policies USING expressions; information_schema.role_table_grants.

title: The complete anon/authenticated PostgREST read surface (everything else is closed)
content: The entire set of public tables a PostgREST role can actually SELECT (grant AND policy both present) is tiny. ANON: blog_posts (policy blog_posts_public_read, USING published=true) and category_specs (policy 'specs readable', USING true). AUTHENTICATED: category_specs (public), documents (policy documents_customer_select, scoped to the caller's own refs — see the customer-isolation record), and five read-only Phase D contract tables: phase_d_gate_contract, phase_d_handler_binding, phase_d_handler_schema, phase_d_payment_state, phase_d_rule_enforcement. brand_assets and the 13 os_owner_admin_read tables have policies but no grant, so they are NOT readable. No table anywhere grants INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to anon or authenticated (has_table_privilege for those = false across the board). anon/authenticated also hold TRIGGER/REFERENCES on a few tables (agent_action_log, legal_documents, templates, undo_log, category_specs) — these are not data-read paths. Net: an attacker with a valid anon key can read published blog posts and category specs; with a customer JWT they additionally read their own documents and the Phase D contract config. Nothing customer-private (customers, inquiries, quotes, transactions, leads, financials) is directly readable via PostgREST tables.
source: information_schema.role_table_grants for anon/authenticated + has_table_privilege confirmations; pg_policies (blog_posts_public_read, 'specs readable', documents_customer_select).

title: SECURITY DEFINER surface: 879 functions owned by postgres (BYPASSRLS) — body is the boundary
content: public holds 879 SECURITY DEFINER functions vs 452 SECURITY INVOKER. ALL 879 are owned by role `postgres`, which is rolbypassrls=true (though NOT a superuser on Supabase — supabase_admin is the superuser). A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the owner's privileges, so every one of these executes as postgres and therefore reads/writes every table with RLS bypassed and full table ownership. This means: for a SECURITY DEFINER RPC, RLS provides ZERO protection — the only things standing between a caller and the data are (1) who holds EXECUTE on the function and (2) the identity/authorization checks written into the function body. This is why the codebase invests so heavily in in-body identity gates (fn_phase_c_require_founder, fn_role_of, ownership joins to fn_customer_document_refs). When reviewing any secdef function here, assume it can do anything to any table and verify the body proves the caller is entitled BEFORE the privileged work. EXECUTE defaults to PUBLIC in Postgres unless revoked, so also confirm the grant surface: anon can EXECUTE 0 secdef functions; authenticated can EXECUTE exactly 7 (next record).
source: pg_proc.prosecdef + pg_roles join (879 secdef, all proowner=postgres, rolbypassrls=true, rolsuper=false); has_function_privilege() EXECUTE counts for anon/authenticated.

title: search_path is pinned on 100% of SECURITY DEFINER functions — the hijack vector is closed
content: The classic SECURITY DEFINER attack is search_path hijacking: if a definer function does not pin search_path, a caller can create a malicious object (e.g. a table or operator named the same as one the function references) in a schema earlier on the path and have the privileged function execute attacker-controlled code. In this database that vector is closed: 879 of 879 SECURITY DEFINER functions set search_path (0 with a null/mutable path). The dominant value is `search_path = public, pg_temp` (538 functions) with pg_temp LAST (the safe position — a caller's temp objects cannot shadow public ones); other pinned variants include `public` (177), `public, pg_catalog` (124), and a few scoped to cron/kb_stage/extensions/net/auth. By contrast, 220 of the 452 SECURITY INVOKER functions lack a pinned path — these are what the advisor's 77 `function_search_path_mutable` lints point at. Because invoker functions run with the caller's (low) privileges, an unpinned path on them is far lower risk than on a definer function. Takeaway: when you write ANY new SECURITY DEFINER function here, you MUST add `SET search_path = public, pg_temp` (or tighter) — the estate-wide invariant is 'every definer function pins its path,' and CI/advisors will flag a regression.
source: pg_proc.proconfig over public: 879/879 secdef pin search_path (0 mutable), 220/452 invoker lack it; distinct search_path value distribution; get_advisors = 77 function_search_path_mutable.

title: The 7 JWT-reachable SECURITY DEFINER RPCs — the privileged PostgREST door
content: anon can EXECUTE 0 SECURITY DEFINER functions. authenticated can EXECUTE exactly 7, and these are the only privileged (RLS-bypassing) operations a caller can trigger via PostgREST with a bearer token: (1) fn_customer_document_refs() and (2) fn_customer_documents(p_q,p_kind,p_lim,p_related_refs) — the customer-portal document read paths, both anchored to the caller's own identity via auth.email()/auth.uid(); (3) fn_founder_command_control(p_command_id,p_op,p_target,p_value,p_actor) and (4) fn_founder_command_clarify(p_command_id,p_answer,p_actor) — founder OS command control; (5) fn_phase_c_founder_subject_bind(p_subject), (6) fn_phase_c_freeze_amendment_approve(p_input jsonb), (7) fn_phase_c_governance_decide(p_input jsonb) — Phase C governance decisions. All 7 pin search_path=public,pg_temp. The founder/governance five each call the hardened founder gate (fn_phase_c_require_founder) as their first act; the customer two constrain rows by an inner join to the caller's own document refs. Supabase's advisor flags these as 7 `authenticated_security_definer_function_executable` — expected and reviewed, not a defect, because each self-authorizes. Any NEW secdef function granted to authenticated joins this exposed set and must carry an equivalent in-body identity check before doing privileged work.
source: pg_proc where prosecdef and has_function_privilege('authenticated',oid,'EXECUTE') = 7 functions listed; anon secdef-executable = 0; get_advisors = 7 authenticated_security_definer_function_executable.

title: fn_phase_c_require_founder — the load-bearing founder-authority gate (PCCR-003/006/007)
content: This SECURITY DEFINER function is the single check that separates 'anyone with a JWT' from 'the founder who can cancel workflows, approve refunds, and decide governance.' Because it runs as postgres, it must prove identity itself; it does so in layers. (1) PCCR-007 connection check FIRST: `if session_user <> 'authenticator' then raise 28000` — a founder call arrives through PostgREST as session_user=authenticator; a migration/management connection (postgres/supabase_admin) is refused, because such a connection can set request.jwt.claims for itself and forge auth.uid(). session_user cannot be changed by the caller (SET ROLE leaves it; SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION is refused). (2) Route A: read auth.uid() and match it against phase_c_founder_identity (active, kind='email'). (3) Route B: a server-verified subject bound via GUC app.phase_c_founder_auth_event, but only if the event's txid = txid_current() (bound to THIS transaction, not a value typed in) AND action_class IS NULL (PCCR-006 purpose-binding: a governance event may not also open the refund door). (4) If no verified identity resolves, raise 28000 — 'knowing the email is not being the founder.' (5) p_actor is treated as an ASSERTION, not a source: if supplied and it disagrees with the verified identity, refuse. The historical bug (memory: 'founder approval is a typed string') where p_actor was trusted is fixed. When touching any founder-authority path, route it through this function; never re-derive founder identity from a caller-supplied string.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_phase_c_require_founder) full body; called as first statement of fn_founder_command_control; memory 'founder approval is a typed string' (the pre-fix state).

title: fn_role_of — the identity resolver behind every role-gated policy
content: fn_role_of(p_email) is a STABLE SECURITY DEFINER function (search_path=public,pg_temp) that maps an email or agent key to a role string used by RLS policies (os_owner_admin_read) and application checks. Resolution order, first match wins: (1) user_roles table — human identities, ordered owner>admin>ops>finance>support>agent, always win; (2) app_secrets key 'admin_emails' (comma list) -> 'owner'; (3) if the value contains NO '@' it is treated as a possible AGENT key: an active org_agents.agent_key returns 'agent', but only when app_secrets 'agent_autonomy_enabled'=true AND current_date >= app_secrets 'agent_autonomy_from' (default 2026-07-30) — otherwise 'guest' (pre-arming behaviour); (4) leads.claimed_by match -> 'supplier'; (5) customers.email match -> 'customer'; else 'guest'. Two design points a security agent must respect: an email can never resolve to 'agent' (the no-'@' guard prevents a human being mistaken for an employee record — memory 'a phone may confirm, never select'), and the function reads app_secrets inside the definer boundary so the admin_email list and autonomy flags never leave the DB. Policies pass auth.jwt()->>'email' into this function; the value therefore comes from the verified JWT, not a caller argument.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_role_of) full body; referenced by os_owner_admin_read policies' USING clause (pg_policies).

title: Customer data isolation: fn_customer_document_refs() + the reveal paywall in the ACL
content: Customer-portal document access is gated by fn_customer_document_refs(), a STABLE SECURITY DEFINER function that derives the caller's OWN customer id from the JWT (`lower(auth.email())` or `auth.uid()` against public.customers) — never from a caller argument. It returns exactly three ref sets: the customer's own inquiry uploads; quote files against their RFQs (excluding status='draft', which customer_api never shows); and supplier documents ONLY for a supplier the customer has PAID to reveal (an inner condition on transactions where revealed_at IS NOT NULL). The RLS policy documents_customer_select on the documents table uses `EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM fn_customer_document_refs() r WHERE r.ref_table=documents.ref_table AND r.ref_id=documents.ref_id)`, and the RPC fn_customer_documents(...) INNER JOINs public.documents to fn_customer_document_refs() — so the caller-supplied p_related_refs argument is only a search filter and cannot widen visibility (no IDOR: passing another customer's refs yields nothing because the join keeps only the caller's own refs). Security consequence: the top-3 reveal paywall is enforced at the DATA layer, not just the UI — a customer literally cannot pull a supplier's certificate/quote documents until transactions.revealed_at is set for that supplier. Preserve this join whenever adding a customer-facing document path.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_customer_document_refs, fn_customer_documents); pg_policies documents_customer_select USING clause; transactions.revealed_at reveal gate.

title: Fully-sealed sensitive tables: secrets and founder identity are unreachable via PostgREST
content: The most sensitive tables are locked at every layer simultaneously — RLS enabled, zero policies, and zero grants to anon/authenticated — so they are unreachable through PostgREST entirely; only service_role edge functions or SECURITY DEFINER functions (running as postgres) can read them. Verified for: app_secrets (holds admin_emails, agent_autonomy_enabled/from, and other operational secrets), user_roles (the human role table fn_role_of trusts first), phase_c_founder_identity and phase_c_founder_auth_event (the founder-auth binding tables), and founder_command (the founder's command ledger). All show rls=true, policies=0, anon/authenticated SELECT=false. customers/leads/transactions also show anon/authenticated SELECT=false (their single os_owner_admin_read policy is inert without a grant). Practical rules: (1) never add an anon/authenticated grant or permissive policy to app_secrets/user_roles/phase_c_* — that would expose the very data the identity system relies on; (2) read these only from inside a definer function or a service_role edge function that has already authorized the caller; (3) app_secrets is the store of record for admin_emails and autonomy flags — changing a value there changes who fn_role_of calls 'owner' and whether agents are armed.
source: Direct check: relrowsecurity + has_table_privilege(anon/authenticated,SELECT) + policy count for app_secrets, user_roles, phase_c_founder_identity, phase_c_founder_auth_event, founder_command, customers, leads, transactions.

title: Views bypass RLS by design — 175 definer views exist but ZERO are PostgREST-exposed
content: public contains 211 views: 175 run as the view owner (definer semantics — they read underlying tables with the owner's privileges and thus bypass the querying role's RLS) and 36 declare security_invoker=true (they honour the caller's RLS). A definer view is a classic RLS-bypass channel: grant one to anon/authenticated and you hand back exactly the rows RLS was withholding. Here that channel is closed at the grant layer — has_table_privilege for BOTH anon and authenticated is FALSE on all 211 views (anon_readable=0, authd_readable=0). So the memory concern that 'a definer view hands back what the table withheld' is currently mitigated: the definer views are used internally (by service_role/definer functions), not exposed to PostgREST roles. The standing rule this implies: if you ever need to expose a view to anon or authenticated, either set `WITH (security_invoker=true)` on it (so RLS on the base tables still applies to the caller) or prove the view's own filter is a complete authorization check — otherwise granting a definer view re-opens every base-table read RLS was closing. Check both reloptions (security_invoker) and the grant before exposing any view.
source: pg_class relkind='v' over public: 211 views, 36 security_invoker, 175 definer; has_table_privilege(anon/authenticated,SELECT) = 0 readable; memory 'a definer view hands back what the table withheld'.

title: Role/BYPASSRLS map: who ignores RLS and how PostgREST assumes roles
content: The roles that matter for this database's access control: anon (rolbypassrls=false, rolcanlogin=false) and authenticated (false, false) are group roles PostgREST switches into; authenticator (rolcanlogin=true, rolinherit=FALSE, rolbypassrls=false) is the login role PostgREST connects as and then SET ROLEs to anon or authenticated (or service_role) based on the verified JWT — its rolinherit=false means it holds no privileges of those roles until it explicitly switches. service_role (rolbypassrls=TRUE, rolcanlogin=false) and postgres (rolbypassrls=TRUE, rolsuper=false) both ignore RLS entirely; postgres additionally owns every table and all 879 definer functions. supabase_admin is the only superuser. Security reasoning that follows: (1) RLS constrains only anon and authenticated — the two roles a public JWT can become; (2) anything running as service_role (all edge functions) or postgres (all definer functions) is outside RLS and must self-authorize in code; (3) session_user reliably distinguishes a PostgREST request (authenticator) from a management/migration connection (postgres/supabase_admin) — fn_phase_c_require_founder depends on exactly this to reject forged founder calls; (4) the founder auth model (mobile OTP -> Supabase JWT) lands the caller as authenticated, so founder-only power is enforced in function bodies, not by a distinct DB role.
source: pg_roles attributes for anon, authenticated, authenticator, service_role, postgres, supabase_admin, supabase_auth_admin (rolsuper/rolbypassrls/rolcanlogin/rolinherit).

title: Extension placement and how to triage the security advisor output
content: Extension hygiene is mostly clean: pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, and pg_stat_statements live in the dedicated `extensions` schema; supabase_vault in `vault`; pg_cron and plpgsql in pg_catalog. Three extensions sit in `public` (the advisor's 3 `extension_in_public` lints): pg_net, pg_trgm, and vector (pgvector). pg_net is the notable one — it provides async outbound HTTP (net.http_post), an SSRF-shaped capability; it is reachable only to roles that can execute it (postgres/service_role), not to anon/authenticated, so exposure is bounded, but treat any function that calls net.* as a potential egress path. When reading get_advisors(security) for this project, triage by design intent: (a) 638 `rls_enabled_no_policy` = the intended default-deny stance, NOT work to do — do not add permissive policies to clear them; (b) 77 `function_search_path_mutable` = all SECURITY INVOKER functions (verified: 0 of 879 definer functions lack a pinned path), so lower risk — still worth pinning opportunistically; (c) 7 `authenticated_security_definer_function_executable` = the reviewed customer/founder RPC surface, each self-authorizing; (d) 3 `extension_in_public` = minor hygiene. The lints that would be REAL defects if they ever appeared: a table with RLS disabled, a definer function with a mutable path, or a sensitive table newly granted to anon/authenticated.
source: pg_extension join pg_namespace (pg_net, pg_trgm, vector in public; others in extensions/vault/pg_catalog); get_advisors(security) lint tallies: 638/77/7/3.

title: The two-door kernel write guard and the kernel_write_authority register
content:
fn_kernel_write_guard is the core write control on the kernel state tables. It is attached as a00_kernel_write_guard / z10_kernel_write_guard BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on 13 tables: kernel_signal_inbox, kernel_trigger_inbox, phase_c_event_outbox, phase_c_founder_auth_event, phase_c_handoff_run, phase_c_refund_decision, phase_c_task, phase_c_workflow_run, phase_c_workflow_step_run, phase_d_capability_request, phase_d_capability_result, phase_d_scenario_record, phase_d_test_context_grant. It admits a write through exactly two doors, else raises 42501.
Door 1 (authorised routine on the stack): it reads GET DIAGNOSTICS v_ctx = PG_CONTEXT and, for each row of public.kernel_write_authority(routine_name, table_name), tests v_ctx ~ 'PL/pgSQL function (public\.)?'||routine_name||'\('. The call stack cannot be forged, so ONLY named kernel primitives (fn_kernel_trigger_submit, fn_kernel_signal_submit, fn_kernel_step_complete, fn_kernel_cancel, fn_kernel_open_step, fn_phase_c_workflow_start, fn_kernel_refund_decision_record, ...) may write. A generic service-role INSERT from an edge function is refused because no authorised routine is on its stack.
Door 2 (audited owner maintenance): current_setting('kernel.maintenance_reason') is non-empty AND current_user = the table owner; the write is logged via fn_kernel_record_maintenance_write. Under SECURITY INVOKER current_user stays the caller's real role, so service_role can never satisfy the owner test. Register = 47 rows over 13 tables.
VERIFY: select table_name, routine_name from kernel_write_authority order by 1; confirm every routine_name still exists in pg_proc (a renamed primitive whose register row was not updated silently loses write access). Re-read the body with pg_get_functiondef('fn_kernel_write_guard'::regproc) to confirm both doors are intact.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_kernel_write_guard); pg_trigger rows a00_kernel_write_guard/z10_kernel_write_guard on 13 tables; public.kernel_write_authority (47 rows, cols routine_name,table_name,why,added_at). Verified live in project htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh.

title: z00_kernel_truncate_guard: closing the TRUNCATE hole around the write guard
content:
TRUNCATE removes every row of a table WITHOUT firing any row-level BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE trigger, so fn_kernel_write_guard never sees it. fn_kernel_truncate_guard closes that hole. It is attached as z00_kernel_truncate_guard BEFORE TRUNCATE on 97 tables (every protected kernel/business table).
Unlike the write guard it has NO Door 1: no kernel routine ever truncates a protected table, so a TRUNCATE is by definition maintenance. The only door is the audited-owner door - current_setting('kernel.maintenance_reason') non-empty AND current_user = pg_tables.tableowner - recorded to kernel_maintenance_write; anything else raises 42501 with the message 'a truncate is not a kernel write and fires no row-level guard'. Since fix K37, stating a reason alone is NOT enough; you must also BE the table owner (service_role is not the owner).
Why it matters for defence: an agent or edge function running as service_role that tried to wipe a table to 'reset' state is refused outright; the only path is a human owner-level maintenance action that leaves an audit row.
VERIFY it is attached everywhere it must be: select c.relname from pg_class c where c.relkind='r' and <table is guarded by a row-guard> except select tgrelid::regclass from pg_trigger where tgname='z00_kernel_truncate_guard'. A table that carries fn_kernel_write_guard or fn_kernel_business_parent_delete_guard but lacks the truncate guard is a bypass. Count check: select count(*) from pg_trigger where tgname='z00_kernel_truncate_guard' and not tgisinternal (expected 97).
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_kernel_truncate_guard); count of z00_kernel_truncate_guard triggers = 97 (pg_trigger). Verified live.

title: Trigger name prefixes encode firing order; verifying a guard is LIVE not just present
content:
Postgres fires BEFORE triggers in alphabetical order by trigger name, and the kernel weaponises that. Prefix conventions on protected tables: a00_/a01_/a05_/a10_ run FIRST (identity, ownership, parent-delete, write-authority, founder-approver, session-verified checks); z00_ is the truncate guard; z10_/z20_ are state-machine / write guards; z50_/z90_/z95_ are emit-to-kernel, decision-trace and mirror steps that must run LAST once the row is accepted. So on a single table you often see a00_kernel_write_guard -> z00_kernel_truncate_guard -> z20_..._state_guard -> z90_..._trace firing in that order.
A disabled trigger and an absent trigger produce the SAME result under a naive COUNT, so a security agent must check enablement explicitly. pg_trigger.tgenabled: 'O'=enabled (fires on origin), 'D'=disabled, 'R'/'A'=replica/always. 
VERIFY the whole guard fabric is live:
1) select tgname, tgrelid::regclass, tgenabled from pg_trigger where not tgisinternal and tgenabled<>'O' and (tgname like 'a0%' or tgname like 'z%' or tgname ilike '%guard%'); -- must be EMPTY (last check: none disabled).
2) Re-derive each guard body with pg_get_functiondef and diff against the committed scripts/sql source; a guard whose body was replaced can report green while enforcing nothing.
3) Never trust a single count: a dropped guard, a disabled guard, and a guard whose predicate can never fire (impossible WHERE) all read as '0 violations'.
source: pg_trigger naming pattern across protected tables (a00_/z00_/z10_/z20_/z90_/z95_); tgenabled semantics; live check returned zero disabled guard triggers. Verified in htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh.

title: Phase A freeze guard: the approved org shape (10/90/86) is digest-locked
content:
fn_phase_a_freeze_guard (trigger z90_phase_a_freeze on org_departments and org_role) protects the founder-approved ORGANISATIONAL SHAPE. It reads the baseline row public.org_phase_baseline where phase='A' and recomputes three live counts: active departments (org_departments where active), canonical roles (org_role status='active' and runtime_mode<>'knowledge_overlay'), and category overlays (org_role status='active' and runtime_mode='knowledge_overlay'). If all three still equal the baseline counts, the statement is not a Phase A change and passes. If any differs, the guard demands set local app.phase_a_change_reason = 'PACR-nnn: <finding, evidence, approver>' in the SAME transaction; without it the statement is refused with the old vs new shape spelled out. With it, the change proceeds and RAISE NOTICE records it.
Approved baseline (frozen 2026-08-15): active_departments=10, canonical_roles=90, category_overlays=86 (also records department_heads=10, organizational_workflows=30, retired_roles=4).
Defence value: an agent that tried to silently add a department or spin up a new canonical role to grant itself scope cannot - the shape is a fixed point and a change without a reason string aborts.
VERIFY: select counts from org_phase_baseline where phase='A'; then run the three counts and compare. Equal = frozen intact. A mismatch with NO corresponding PACR file in scripts/sql/ is drift that slipped through (only possible if the guard was disabled - see the tgenabled check).
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_phase_a_freeze_guard); org_phase_baseline phase='A' counts jsonb {active_departments:10, canonical_roles:90, category_overlays:86,...}. Verified live.

title: Phase B freeze guard: workflow architecture locked by per-subject SHA-256 digest
content:
fn_phase_b_freeze_guard (trigger z90_phase_b_freeze on the phase_b_* tables: phase_b_workflow, phase_b_workflow_step, phase_b_gate, phase_b_business_rule, phase_b_handoff, phase_b_step_state/transition, phase_b_workflow_state/transition, phase_b_dynamic_actor, phase_b_founder_boundary) protects the approved BUSINESS-WORKFLOW ARCHITECTURE. Unlike Phase A (which compares counts), Phase B compares CONTENT digests: it calls public.fn_phase_b_structure_digest(), which emits a sha256 per subject, and compares each to the value stored at approval in org_phase_baseline.registry_sha256->'structure'-><subject>->>'database'. Any subject whose live sha256 differs is named in the error ('<subject> (<live12> != <baseline12>)'). To proceed you must set local app.phase_b_change_reason = 'PBCR-nnn: <problem, evidence, current workflow/step, proposed change, owners, state-machine impact, gate/rule impact, customer/supplier/privacy/legal/financial impact, backward compat, founder-approval?>' in the same transaction; otherwise refused.
Approved 2026-08-15 as the final QuotesDone workflow design.
Defence value: the digest catches a SINGLE changed step/gate/rule that a count would miss - editing one gate's condition moves that subject's hash.
VERIFY: select d.subject, d.sha256, b.registry_sha256->'structure'->d.subject->>'database' as baseline from fn_phase_b_structure_digest() d cross join (select registry_sha256 from org_phase_baseline where phase='B') b; every row should match. A mismatch with no PBCR file = drift.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_phase_b_freeze_guard); fn_phase_b_structure_digest() drives comparison against org_phase_baseline.registry_sha256->'structure'. Verified live.

title: org_phase_baseline is append-only: the fixed point the drift checks measure against
content:
The Phase A and Phase B freeze guards both read public.org_phase_baseline as their reference. That baseline is itself protected by fn_org_phase_baseline_append_only (trigger a00_org_phase_baseline_append_only), which raises 23514 on ANY INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE - the rows are the founder-approved record of what a phase WAS when approved, and four drift checks read them as the fixed point. If a baseline row could be freely edited, an attacker could move the goalposts and make live drift 'match' a rewritten past.
Amending a baseline is deliberate and procedural, not a plain UPDATE: write scripts/sql/pacr_NNN_<what_and_why>.sql (or pbcr_) that (1) DROP TRIGGER a00_org_phase_baseline_append_only, (2) makes the change with EVERY digest RECOMPUTED in place (not hand-typed), (3) recreates the trigger in the SAME transaction, and (4) is appended to scripts/sql/MANIFEST.txt. The dropped-and-recreated trigger inside that file is the durable record that the freeze was opened on purpose.
Defence value: the baseline is the anchor; making it append-only means the only way to change 'what was approved' leaves a committed, named migration behind.
VERIFY: select tgname, tgenabled from pg_trigger where tgname='a00_org_phase_baseline_append_only' (must be 'O'); and any change to baseline content must correspond to a pacr_/pbcr_ file in scripts/sql/MANIFEST.txt.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_org_phase_baseline_append_only); memory note 'org_phase_baseline is append-only'. Verified live.

title: Action-authority tiers: org_authority.max_tier and fn_authority_rank (fail-closed)
content:
The advisory/gated/supervised/autonomous tiers are NOT stored on org_action_executor (a common misread); they live on public.org_authority(dept_key, action_class, max_tier, threshold_aed, note) - one row per department per action_class. This is the matrix that answers 'how much unsupervised power does THIS department have over THIS action_class?'.
fn_authority_rank(text) IMMUTABLE ranks the tiers: advisory=0 (advises only), gated=1 (needs approval before acting), supervised=2 (acts, reviewed after), autonomous=3 (acts unreviewed). Any UNKNOWN tier returns 3 - it ranks HIGHEST so that fail-closed logic treats an unrecognised tier as maximally powerful and demands justification to set it.
Money is bounded by threshold_aed: e.g. finance/money_move=gated:10000, payments/money_move=gated, growth|marketing/ad_spend=gated, and the legacy customer_experience|customer_success/refund_within_window=autonomous:2000. NOTE the refund exception below: despite that autonomous:2000 row, the refunds table guard now forces founder approval at ANY amount - org_authority is not the last word on refunds. Deploy tiers: production_deploy=gated everywhere; code_selfheal/incident_fix are supervised or autonomous only in engineering/it/assurance/product_eng.
VERIFY a department's real ceiling: select max_tier, threshold_aed from org_authority where dept_key=$1 and action_class=$2; and read the runtime rank with fn_authority_rank(max_tier). To audit an unexpected autonomous grant: select * from org_authority where max_tier='autonomous' order by dept_key.
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_authority_rank); org_authority rows (cols dept_key,action_class,max_tier,threshold_aed,note); sample incl finance/money_move=gated:10000, refund_within_window=autonomous:2000. Verified live.

title: org_authority_guard + app.change_reason: widening a tier is audited, tightening is free
content:
fn_org_authority_guard (SECURITY DEFINER, trigger trg_org_authority_guard on org_authority) enforces the standing pattern for privilege changes: raising power needs a stated reason, lowering never does, and every change is logged. On UPDATE/INSERT it computes v_widen = fn_authority_rank(new.max_tier) > fn_authority_rank(coalesce(old.max_tier,'advisory')) OR new.threshold_aed > old.threshold_aed. A DELETE is always a tighten (removing a permission). If v_widen and current_setting('app.change_reason') is null or shorter than 12 chars, it raises check_violation demanding: set local app.change_reason = 'why, in a sentence'; in the same transaction. Every operation - widen or tighten - inserts a row into public.autonomy_control_audit(object, op, direction, old_value, new_value, reason), object = 'org_authority:'||dept_key||'/'||action_class.
This is the SAME shape used by fn_autonomy_control_guard on app_secrets: an edge function running PostgREST cannot set a local GUC, so it structurally cannot widen authority - only a deliberate session that states a reason can, and the reason is captured.
Defence value: no silent privilege escalation; the audit table is the tamper-evident ledger of who widened what and why.
VERIFY recent authority changes: select object, direction, old_value, new_value, reason, created_at from autonomy_control_audit where object like 'org_authority:%' order by created_at desc; a 'widen' row with a null/blank reason should be impossible (its presence means the guard was bypassed or disabled).
source: pg_get_functiondef(fn_org_authority_guard); writes autonomy_control_audit; mirrors fn_autonomy_control_guard. Verified live.

title: The autonomy kill-switch trio and fn_autonomy_control_guard on app_secrets
content:
Four keys in public.app_secrets are the master brakes on the AI workforce: agent_autonomy_enabled ('true' to allow broad autonomy), agent_autonomy_from (date autonomy is permitted from), cos_frozen ('true' halts the Chief-of-Staff executor), ai_kill_switch (set halts everything). fn_autonomy_status() STABLE returns {allowed, blockers[], checked_at}: allowed is true only when agent_autonomy_enabled='true', cos_frozen<>'true', ai_kill_switch is false/null, agent_autonomy_from is not in the future, and NO priority-0 spec_backlog rows are open. It fails closed - any error makes allowed=false.
fn_autonomy_control_guard (SECURITY DEFINER, trigger trg_autonomy_control_guard on app_secrets) governs changes to those four keys: WIDENING autonomy (enabling the flag, un-freezing, clearing the kill switch, moving the from-date) requires set local app.change_reason (>=12 chars) in the same transaction; TIGHTENING (freeze, kill, disable) never needs a reason and is never refused. Every change lands in autonomy_control_audit. Because a PostgREST update from an edge function cannot set that local GUC, the ~190 service-role functions that can reach app_secrets structurally cannot turn autonomy ON - which is the point.
VERIFY current posture: select fn_autonomy_status(); select key, value from app_secrets where key in ('agent_autonomy_enabled','agent_autonomy_from','cos_frozen','ai_kill_switch'); and audit the history in autonomy_control_audit where object like 'app_secrets:%'.
