- app_secrets table: simple, RLS deny-all so only service_role/edge functions read it, but values are PLAINTEXT at rest — visible in a base backup, a pg_dump, or to anyone who gains service_role or DB-owner access.
- Vault (`vault.create_secret` / `vault.decrypted_secrets`): authenticated-encryption at rest via pgsodium; the ciphertext in a dump is useless without the key. Preferred for high-value secrets.
Either way, the non-negotiable discipline (done well in stripe_webhook): secrets are NEVER logged — the code records only 'which mode verified', never the key. Recall memory 'redact before you truncate' — redact the value, not just its length.
Hardening checklist: (1) inventory every secret and where it is read; (2) migrate high-value keys (Stripe secret key, OpenRouter key, Twilio auth token) to Vault or keep them purely in edge-function env, not the DB; (3) scan logs (Supabase, Vercel, agent_runs) for accidental secret material; (4) rotate on any exposure.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/stripe_webhook/index.ts (app_secrets reads) and list_extensions showing supabase_vault 0.3.1 installed, unused for these secrets, on htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh.

title: pg_net / http extensions turn the database into an SSRF pivot
content:
`pg_net` (async HTTP) is installed at 0.20.3 in the `public` schema on this project; the synchronous `http` extension is available but NOT installed (keep it that way). Any code path that lets an attacker or an LLM agent influence a URL passed to `net.http_get/http_post` gives them Server-Side Request Forgery FROM inside Postgres — reachable targets include cloud metadata endpoints, internal Supabase services, and other private hosts the DB can route to. Because these calls originate from the trusted DB network, they bypass perimeter controls.

Risk here is amplified by the AI agent workforce: agents assemble outbound calls, and DB triggers/crons emit HTTP. If any destination is derived from customer inquiry text, supplier data, or model output, treat it as attacker-controllable.

Hardening:
1. Move pg_net out of `public` into a dedicated `extensions`/`net` schema and `REVOKE EXECUTE ON ... FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;` — only trusted definer routines should call it.
2. Allowlist destination hosts in the wrapper routine; reject private/link-local ranges (169.254.169.254, 10/8, 127/8, ::1) and non-https.
3. Never let a caller/agent pass a raw URL; pass an enum of known endpoints and build the URL server-side.
4. Do not install `http`, `dblink`, or `postgres_fdw` unless required — each is another egress/SSRF path.
source: list_extensions on htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh: pg_net 0.20.3 installed in public, http not installed; classic DB-SSRF class + cloud metadata SSRF (169.254.169.254).

title: Postgres extension attack surface — what's dangerous if ever enabled, and the 3 in public
content:
Every enabled extension widens the trusted surface. Installed today (keep reviewing): pgcrypto, pg_stat_statements, uuid-ossp, pg_cron 1.6.4, pg_net 0.20.3, vector 0.8.0, pg_trgm, supabase_vault, plpgsql. Advisor flags 3 `extension_in_public` WARNs — `vector`, `pg_net`, `pg_trgm` sit in `public`. Extensions in `public` combine badly with mutable search_path (their functions become shadowing/qualification hazards) and clutter the API schema; move them to `extensions` where practical.

High-risk extensions to NOT enable unless truly needed (each is a known escalation/egress class):
- `http` — synchronous SSRF from the DB (see pg_net record).
- `dblink` / `postgres_fdw` — outbound connections, credential handling, SSRF.
- `xml2` — XPath/XSLT with XXE and file-read history.
- `file_fdw` / `lo` / `adminpack` — filesystem reach.
- untrusted PLs (`plpython3u`, `plperlu`) — arbitrary code as the DB OS user; not installed, keep it so.
- `pg_cron` (installed) runs jobs as a superuser-ish role — audit `cron.job` for who can schedule and what commands run (recall 'the cron command no longer names the routine' — jobs call fn_kernel_cron_exec(jobid)).
Hardening: treat `CREATE EXTENSION` as a privileged change requiring review; pin extension schemas; re-run get_advisors after any extension change.
source: list_extensions on htdblwldjkcgjvmqkbeh 2026-09-02; Supabase linter 0014 extension_in_public (3 WARN: vector/pg_net/pg_trgm); general PostgreSQL untrusted-language/XXE risk classes.

title: Deno edge-runtime hardening: JWT gating, import integrity, and pinned dependencies
content:
Supabase edge functions run on Deno. Two distinct concerns:
1. AuthZ at the edge: each function has a `verify_jwt` setting (config.toml / dashboard). Public endpoints (webhooks, public pages) legitimately disable it BUT must then do their own auth — Stripe/Twilio signature checks, or an explicit token check. A function that both disables verify_jwt AND holds service_role AND takes a caller-supplied id is a full-authz-bypass waiting to happen. Inventory every function: verify_jwt state x does-it-hold-service_role x does-it-trust-caller-input. Our webhook does this correctly (signature verify before any effect); audit the other 208.
2. Supply chain: Deno imports resolve from `jsr:`, `npm:`, and `https:` URLs. We import `jsr:@supabase/supabase-js@2` — a FLOATING major; a compromised or breaking 2.x publish lands automatically. Pin to exact versions and commit a `deno.lock` so integrity hashes are enforced on every deploy; unpinned URL imports are the dependency-confusion/typosquat vector. Review third-party import hosts; prefer jsr/npm over arbitrary https.
Hardening: pin+lock all imports; keep verify_jwt ON unless the function self-authenticates; least-privilege — a function that doesn't need service_role should use the anon/user client so RLS still applies.
source: Supabase Edge Functions verify_jwt/config docs; Deno permissions & lockfile integrity model; import `jsr:@supabase/supabase-js@2` observed in supabase/functions/stripe_webhook.

title: Next.js CVE patterns vs our reality: middleware is NOT our auth gate
content:
Next.js has a recurring class of framework-level auth/SSRF bugs — know them, then check where WE actually enforce authz:
- CVE-2025-29927: middleware authorization BYPASS via a forged `x-middleware-subrequest` header; any app that gated auth in `middleware.ts` was bypassable (fixed 14.2.25 / 15.2.3). 
- CVE-2024-34351: SSRF in Server Actions via the Host header on redirect.
- CVE-2024-46982: cache-poisoning of SSR pages. Plus recurring Image Optimization SSRF/DoS advisories.
Our mapping: `src/middleware.ts` is `next-intl` locale routing ONLY (createMiddleware(routing)) — it performs NO authorization. That is the correct posture: it means a middleware-bypass CVE cannot bypass our auth, because auth lives at the data layer (Supabase RLS + JWT-verifying edge functions), not the edge/middleware. Keep it that way — do not migrate auth INTO middleware. Running Next 16.2.x (past the 29927 fix line), but the class recurs.
Hardening: keep authz in RLS/edge functions; on every Next upgrade read the security notes and run `npm audit`; if Server Actions or the Image Optimizer are used, restrict `images.remotePatterns`/domains to an allowlist; never trust `Host`/`X-Forwarded-*` for security decisions.
source: Next.js security advisories (GHSA for CVE-2025-29927, CVE-2024-34351, CVE-2024-46982); grounded in src/middleware.ts (next-intl only) and Next 16.2.11 in node_modules.

title: npm / React dependency supply chain — audit, pin, and postinstall discipline
content:
The frontend's real risk is not our code but the transitive tree (Next, next-intl, radix-ui, zustand, framer-motion and their deps). Vulnerability classes: prototype pollution, ReDoS in parsers, XSS in render helpers, and outright malicious packages (the 2024-2025 npm compromise wave — hijacked maintainer accounts pushing credential-stealing `postinstall` scripts, typosquats, and dependency-confusion against internal names).

Hardening / refresh (runnable):
- `npm audit` + `npm audit --omit=dev` in CI, failing the build on high/critical; `npm audit fix` for safe bumps, `overrides` to force a fixed transitive version when a direct dep lags.
- `npm ci` from a committed lockfile only — never an unpinned `npm install` in CI. This project uses a Deno-managed npm layout (`node_modules/.deno/...`); the same pin+lock discipline applies to it.
- Consider `--ignore-scripts` for install in CI to neutralize malicious `postinstall`, running only vetted build steps explicitly.
- Turn on GitHub Dependabot alerts + version-update PRs; triage weekly.
- Watch for dependency confusion: any internal/scoped package name must be reserved on the public registry or scoped so it can't be shadowed.
Remember: a green build is not a safe tree — audit runs against a feed that updates daily, so re-run it, don't cache the verdict.
source: npm audit / GitHub Dependabot tooling; 2024-2025 npm maintainer-compromise incidents; package tree observed (next 16.2.11, next-intl 4.13.4, radix-ui, zustand) in node_modules/.deno.

title: Webhook signature verification and replay — the Stripe pattern to copy for Twilio
content:
Any endpoint that acts on a POST from Stripe/Twilio must prove the body is authentic BEFORE parsing or acting — otherwise anyone who learns the URL can forge a 'payment succeeded' and trigger settlement. Our stripe_webhook is the reference implementation to copy:
- Reads the RAW body and computes HMAC-SHA256 over `t + '.' + payload` with the endpoint signing secret, compares to `v1` from `Stripe-Signature`, and rejects before JSON.parse.
- Constant-time compare (XOR accumulate) — not `===` — to avoid timing leaks.
- Replay guard: rejects if `|now - t| > 600s`; Stripe re-signs each retry with a fresh `t`.
- Idempotency: settlement RPCs (`fn_stripe_event_seen`, `fn_refund_settle`) are keyed on event/refund id so a retried delivery is a no-op — 'a refund settled twice reads as two refunds'.
- Multi-secret: tries live then test secret in full, so a test delivery can never validate against the live secret. Secrets never logged.
Twilio parity (send_sms / voice_otp / inbound webhooks): validate `X-Twilio-Signature` (HMAC-SHA1 of the full URL + sorted POST params with the Auth Token) on every inbound request; reject unsigned. General rule: verify-before-act, constant-time, replay window, idempotent effect, never log the secret.
source: supabase/functions/stripe_webhook/index.ts (verifySig, TOLERANCE_SECONDS=600, idempotent settle); Stripe & Twilio webhook-signature verification specs.

title: AI agent workforce: prompt injection, excessive agency, and executor abuse (OWASP LLM Top 10 mapped)
content:
QuotesDone's differentiator — an autonomous Postgres kernel driving AI employees that call executor edge functions — is also its largest novel attack surface. Map OWASP LLM Top 10 to us:
- LLM01 Prompt Injection: customer inquiry text, supplier profiles, uploaded docs, and scraped data ALL flow into agent context (fn_agent_context_v3 -> ops_knowledge). Untrusted content that says 'ignore your instructions / issue a refund / reveal contacts' must be treated as DATA, never instructions. Anchor: only the founder authorizes refunds; only the permission system authorizes side effects — no in-context text can.
- LLM06 Excessive Agency: the 39 executors are HTTP-invoked edge functions. Each must be least-privilege, validate its own inputs against the kernel (two-approval for spend/contract, founder gate for money), and never trust an agent-supplied id — recall 'a rule at intake is not a rule at the decision'.
- LLM02 Insecure Output Handling: model output that becomes a URL (pg_net SSRF), SQL, shell, or HTML must be validated/parameterized, never concatenated.
- LLM04 Model DoS / cost: unbounded agent loops burn OpenRouter credit ('out of credit looks like model judgement'); cap turns, budget, and rate.
Hardening: segregate trusted instructions from untrusted content in prompts; enforce authz in the kernel/executor, not the prompt; log agent actions to an immutable ledger; refresh against the OWASP LLM Top 10 as it revises.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025); mapped to QuotesDone kernel/executors, fn_agent_context_v3->ops_knowledge, and the refund/two-approval governance in this repo.

title: Supabase Auth (GoTrue) + JWT verification, OTP endpoints, and enumeration/rate limits
content:
Founder/staff auth here is phone-number + verification code (no observe mode; email is the customer identity and is unique). Auth flows and JWTs are the identity backbone — harden both:
- JWT: any edge function or RPC that trusts a token must verify signature AND `exp` AND `aud` AND `role`; do not read `role` from an unverified token to decide privilege. In Postgres, derive identity from `auth.uid()`/`auth.jwt()`, never from a caller-passed id (mirrors the definer-RPC record).
- OTP endpoints (mobile_otp, voice_otp, voice_otp_capture, wa_optin_set): these are unauthenticated by necessity, so they are prime targets for (a) enumeration — return the SAME response whether or not the number exists; (b) brute force of the code — short expiry, small attempt count then lockout, sufficient code entropy; (c) SMS/voice pumping — rate-limit per number and per IP, cap spend. 'A phone may confirm, never select': a phone number authenticates an existing identity, it must not create or pick one.
- Supabase Auth settings to check via get_advisors/dashboard: leaked-password protection, secure email/phone change, OTP expiry, and disabling anon sign-ups if unused.
- GoTrue itself gets CVEs — track the Supabase platform changelog and the auth server version on refresh.
source: Supabase Auth/GoTrue + JWT model; OTP endpoints observed (mobile_otp, voice_otp, voice_otp_capture); memory rules 'a phone may confirm never select' and 'no observe mode — plain login'.

title: Log and error hygiene across Supabase, edge functions, and Vercel
content:
Logs are a soft data-exfiltration and secret-leak channel, and the AI workforce writes a LOT of them (agent_runs, notifications, kernel ledgers). Threats and hardening:
- Secret material in logs: audit that no function logs the service_role key, Stripe/Twilio/OpenRouter secrets, or full JWTs. stripe_webhook models the right discipline — it logs 'which mode verified', never the secret. Recall 'redact before you truncate' (redact the value, not just cap its length) and 'an error string that was our own timeout' (our own diagnostics leaking internal detail).
- PII in logs: customer emails/phones and inquiry contents landing in Vercel/Supabase logs are a PDPL exposure; minimize and redact. QuotesDone is UAE/GCC-scoped (PDPL), so data-locality and retention of logs matter — keep them in-region and time-boxed.
- Error responses to clients: never return raw exception text, stack traces, or DB messages to anon callers — they leak schema and internal structure. Return a generic message + a correlation id; keep detail server-side.
- Refresh: periodically grep production logs (Supabase log explorer, `query_logs`, Vercel runtime logs) for key prefixes and email/phone patterns; alert on any hit. Sweep GitHub Actions/Vercel/Supabase at end of session (standing rule).
source: stripe_webhook 'never log the secret' pattern; memory 'redact before you truncate' and end-of-session log sweep; UAE PDPL data-locality scope.

title: SLI/SLO catalog for the QuotesDone marketplace
content:
Define reliability by the user journey that earns money, not by CPU graphs. The four SLOs that matter here:
1. Inquiry-to-reveal path availability. The revenue funnel is inquiry_intake -> route_inquiry/dispatch_inquiry -> inquiry_matches -> quote_compare -> reveal (reveal_invoices). SLI = fraction of inquiries that reach a revealable top-3 within their SLA window. Target 99.5% of inquiries reach reveal-ready < 24h. Measure from inquiries + inquiry_matches + reveal_invoices, not from an edge-function 200.
2. Payment success rate. SLI = successful Stripe checkouts / attempted (stripe_checkout, stripe_confirm, stripe_webhook, transactions). Target >= 99% excluding customer card declines. A dip is a payments outage, page immediately - this is the only path that takes money.
3. Agent-run success. SLI = agent_runs.status='ok' / total per agent per day. Crons and edge jobs all log here. Target >= 98% for money/notification agents (send_outbox, stripe_webhook, email_cron), softer for enrichment.
4. Notification delivery. Reveal fires 2 emails + 2 WhatsApps (founder rule); SLI = sent/queued in notifications + outbox. 
Write these as error budgets: 99.5% monthly = ~3.6h of funnel unavailability. Spend budget on deploys; freeze deploys when exhausted. Today production still has near-zero live inquiries, so bootstrap SLOs from synthetic probes (resilience_ping, uptime_check, §8 harness) until real volume exists - a 100% success rate over 0 events is not a measurement.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/{inquiry_intake,dispatch_inquiry,quote_compare,stripe_checkout,stripe_webhook}, agent_runs table, and MEMORY 'reveal notifies both parties'. Method: Google SRE Book (SLIs/SLOs/error budgets).

title: agent_runs is the observability spine (and a cron log, not an employee log)
content:
Every cron and internal edge function writes one row to public.agent_runs: {agent, started_at, finished_at, status, counts jsonb, note text}. status is 'ok' or 'error'; counts is the structured per-run tally (e.g. {authorised, bad_or_missing_secret} on an auth reject, {sent, deduped} on a mailer); note is a <=500-char human sentence, often explaining WHY zero work happened. This is the first place to look in any incident - it is the closest thing to structured logs the platform keeps outside Supabase's own log tables.
Run-ledger discipline used across the codebase: wrap the insert in try/catch so logging can never break the function ('never let logging break the function'), log a row even on the auth-reject path (so a scanner probing an old hole is visible), and put the reason a job did nothing into counts/note rather than a string literal that is read once.
Critical trap: agent_runs is a CRON/execution log, NOT a roster of the AI workforce. 75 of 93 AI employees have never executed anything, so counting distinct agent_runs.agent under-reports the org and over-reports health. To ask 'is this scheduled job alive?' use fn_cron_ran(jobname, within) / fn_cron_liveness against pg_cron's own run history, not a watermark over agent_runs (a shared-table row delta is not attribution to one job).
source: Grounded in the logRun() pattern across supabase/functions/*/index.ts and MEMORY 'agent_runs is a cron log not an employee log' + 'a guard that counted a cron job's rows'.

title: Cron liveness and the external dead-man's-watchdog (resilience_ping)
content:
All scheduled automation runs on Supabase pg_cron via fn_kernel_cron_exec(jobid) (22 of 23 active jobs call it, one indirection so the command no longer names the routine). The failure mode that internal monitoring CANNOT catch is the scheduler itself dying: if pg_cron stops, every internal health cron stops too, so nothing pages.
The fix is a two-tier dead-man's switch. fn_cron_liveness returns {healthy, newest_run_age_min} by reading pg_cron's run history with a plain SELECT (works while Postgres is up even if pg_cron stopped scheduling). resilience_ping is an HTTP edge function hit every ~15min by an EXTERNAL scheduler (a GitHub Action / uptime service) - it survives a total pg_cron outage because it is not itself a cron. If no job has run in >20min it pages the founder DIRECTLY over HTTP (alert_founder -> WhatsApp) and force-flushes the outbox, so the alert escapes even with pg_net/pg_cron down. It is public and secretless by design (returns only liveness, pages only when genuinely down, deduped 30min via app_secrets.cron_down_last_alert) so any external monitor can wire it with just the URL.
Rule an operator must internalize: a monitor that depends on the thing it monitors is not a monitor. The watchdog for the scheduler must live outside the scheduler.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/resilience_ping/index.ts, fn_cron_liveness (migration 20260724014606), and MEMORY 'the cron command no longer names the routine'.

title: AI-provider health monitoring: page on the transition, not on every failure
content:
ai_health is a lightweight liveness monitor for the inference gateway. It pings OpenRouter's free /key endpoint (no tokens spent) to confirm the gateway + API key are reachable, run by the ai_health_15min cron. Two design choices every alerting system should copy:
1. Page on the EDGE, not the level. It raises a deduped operator alert only on the transition INTO an outage - after 2 consecutive failures (THRESHOLD=2), tracked in app_secrets.ai_health_fails - and logs recovery when it returns. One flaky probe never pages; a real outage pages once, not every 15 minutes.
2. Zero-cost aware. The founder holds every OpenRouter route open-circuit until he releases it; when held, a paid liveness ping would either fail or spend, so the job must not treat 'we chose not to call the paid provider' as an outage. 'Out of credit looks like model judgement' and 'every model route is open-circuit' are the two states a health check must distinguish from a genuine provider-down.
Security note that is also a reliability note: ai_health is secret-gated and fails CLOSED (requireInternal). An earlier bug accepted an empty POST and let an anonymous caller write app_secrets.ai_health_fails - hammering it while OpenRouter was healthy could drive the counter down and SUPPRESS the paging transition, hiding a real outage. A monitor whose state an attacker can write is not a monitor.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/ai_health/index.ts (THRESHOLD, ai_health_fails, requireInternal) and MEMORY 'out of credit looks like model judgement' + 'the hold is on routes'.

title: Paging discipline: the actionability gate and WhatsApp escalation (alert_founder)
content:
alert_founder is the single paging channel. Body {event, detail?, level?, force?, dedupe_key?}. It ALWAYS logs to founder_alerts, but only NOTIFIES when the alert is actionable: level in {warn, warning, critical, error, high, urgent, action, danger, fail, failed, alert, escalation} or force:true. Info/ok/healthy are logged and silently suppressed - the founder only hears about things that need a decision. This is the primary defense against alert fatigue in a one-human-on-call company.
Escalation tiers by channel: critical/urgent/high/danger go out over WhatsApp (send_whatsapp) AND branded email; lower actionable levels email only. WhatsApp is the founder's command channel - he runs the company by texting - so reserve it for what genuinely needs him now.
Dedup: if the same event (or dedupe_key) was emailed in the last 6h, it is logged as channel='deduped' and no repeat email is sent. Always pass a stable dedupe_key for recurring conditions so a stuck job does not send hourly.
Operator rules: (1) choose the level honestly - crying 'critical' for a retryable blip trains the human to ignore the channel; (2) the alert text must say what was detected and what to do (it links to quotesdone.com/os to act); (3) alert_founder is secret-gated (requireInternal, fail-closed) precisely because an open pager is a DoS-by-notification vector.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/alert_founder/index.ts (ACTIONABLE set, WhatsApp tiering, 6h dedup) and MEMORY 'WhatsApp is the founder's command channel'.

title: Backup architecture, RPO, and what is actually being backed up
content:
The `backup` edge function dumps core tables to the Supabase Storage 'backups' bucket, stamped by DATE, as pages: `${stamp}/${table}/page_NNNN.json`. Two hard-won constraints:
1. Add invocations, never batch size. Dumping a whole table into one array before JSON.stringify peaks at one-table-plus-its-JSON of memory and dies with HTTP 546 WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT as the estate grows (kb_chunks is ~105,920 rows). It now uploads each 1,000-row page as it reads it (peak memory ~1,000 rows) and is RESUMABLE AT PAGE granularity - a slice can stop mid-table and the next invocation resumes at the exact page - because one table (kb_chunks ~96-105 pages) already exceeds a single worker's ~100s budget. On a same-day re-run it first clears the table's prefix (uploads upsert; a shorter re-run would otherwise leave stale pages that dr_drill would concatenate into a restore that never existed).
2. Back up what the company actually owns. The revenue tables (customers, inquiries, quotes, transactions) are empty today; the real value is the KNOWLEDGE ESTATE - kb_chunks, agent_knowledge, dept_library (UAE domain reference), ops_knowledge (founder-supplied operational records), leads. These were once silently NOT in the snapshot. Verify the FULL[] list still covers them.
RPO: this JSON snapshot is coarse (daily). Supabase PITR is the real low-RPO layer (WAL-based, near-continuous). Treat `backup` as a portable, restore-drillable, off-Postgres copy (survives a project-level loss), and PITR as the primary RPO<=minutes control. Know which one you are relying on before an incident, not during.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/backup/index.ts (FULL[], dumpTablePaged, 546 history) and MEMORY 'the knowledge estate was not backed up'. Method: RPO/RTO from ITIL/SRE DR practice; Supabase PITR docs.

title: Disaster-recovery restore drills: a backup you have not restored is a hypothesis
content:
dr_drill is the only assertion that the company's backups are restorable. It downloads the backup JSON pages, reloads them into public.dr_restore, and reports backup-vs-live row counts plus a schema-key integrity check (each table carries a required key column). It is the RTO half of DR: a snapshot nobody has ever reloaded proves nothing.
Two failure classes it has already taught:
- Format drift. When `backup` moved to `${stamp}/${table}/page_NNNN.json`, the drill still read `${day}/${table}.json` and reported `backup_missing` for every table - the restore test was silently failing wholesale while the green count came from the drill measuring the wrong path. A restore drill must track the backup's on-disk layout exactly, and must fail loudly (not read 0) when it can't find files.
- Worker limits. Restoring is heavier than dumping; all three naive shapes died at HTTP 546 (~60-110s). The drill now chains at PAGE granularity carrying {table index, page index, rows restored} with SLICE_MS=25000 and MAX_HOPS=60, matching backup's own page-resume model.
Also drill what EXISTS, not just the revenue path: five of the six original tables are empty in production, so drilling only those made `total_restored: 1` - structurally incapable of catching a real corruption. Keep the revenue path for the day customers arrive AND drill the knowledge estate that has value now.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/dr_drill/index.ts (TABLES[], SLICE_MS, MAX_HOPS, page-resume) and its own header on the page-format-drift bug.

title: Safe-deploy control: apply then read the definition back out
content:
The deploy discipline for database routines is an operational control, not a style choice. scripts/apply_sql.mjs applies a .sql file and then VERIFIES BY READING pg_get_functiondef BACK OUT of the live database - a POST returning 200 is NOT proof the routine is live and correct; only the read-back is. Since staging was deleted (15 Aug 2026) there is ONE project, so the read-back happens after the apply instead of between two projects, and it is what makes the exit code mean something.
Controls baked in: (1) DRY RUN is the default - a bare `node apply_sql.mjs x.sql` runs guards and writes nothing; you must add --apply (or its history alias --promote) to write production. With no rehearsal copy left, an accidental live write is the risk the default guards against. (2) --ddl prints the public-schema shape digest either side of the apply, because pg_get_functiondef cannot express columns/views/cron rows, so a file meant to add a column that didn't says so instead of exiting 0 on an empty routine list. (3) Parity gates (verify_prod_parity, canonical_routines, sql_files_match_live) assert the repo files match live; every new scripts/sql file needs a MANIFEST line or canonical_routines goes red.
War-story rules: 'promote carries the definition, not the grants' - re-applying a MANIFEST file can silently revert a GRANT; the read-back covers bodies, not grants. 'Green PR does not mean deployable.' Regenerate the mirror after the LAST apply.
source: Grounded in scripts/apply_sql.mjs header and scripts/checks/{canonical_routines,verify_prod_parity}. MEMORY 'the read-back covers bodies not grants', 'green PR does not mean deployable', 'regenerate the mirror after the last apply'.

title: Frozen-phase and change-request discipline as change management
content:
Parts of the kernel are FROZEN: Phase C and Phase D routines and the two org_phase baselines cannot be edited freely. A real fix to a frozen routine is still a governed change - restore the frozen subject and raise the change request (a PACR for the org/phase baseline, a PBCR for workflow behaviour; an owner/reviewer change touches BOTH baselines, i.e. a combined PACR+PBCR). The Phase D acceptance standard is itself frozen: one document, two open gates, and no audit may add a gate or move the bar.
Why this is an ops control and not bureaucracy: in an autonomous company the agents themselves propose changes, so an unguarded 'just fix it' path lets a routine rewrite the rules that govern it. The change-request gates are the equivalent of a production change-approval board - they force a diff to a frozen invariant to be visible, reviewed, and reversible before it lands. org_phase_baseline is APPEND-ONLY: a PACR must drop a00_org_phase_baseline_append_only, recompute digests in place, and recreate the guard in the SAME transaction - never leave the append-only guard off across a commit boundary.
Operator rule: before editing anything under scripts/sql/phase_c* or phase_d*, check whether it is frozen and route through the change request. A tightened guard also reddens its own probes ('tightening a guard reddens its own probes') - expect and account for that, don't paper over it.

title: Cost and capacity as an operational AND security signal (OpenRouter spend)
content:
AI spend is the platform's main variable cost and a live anomaly detector. ai_gateway meters every model call into ai_cost_log from model_registry pricing (including cache-read pricing); cost_snapshot rolls up real OpenRouter spend + revenue weekly (cost_snapshot_weekly cron) and emails the founder. Read spend three ways:
1. Capacity/cost. 94% of spend is INPUT tokens, so the biggest lever is prompt caching (cache_control:{type:'ephemeral'} on system prefixes >~1k tokens; below that the 1.25x write premium beats the 10x read discount only at real hit rates). The large model tier is ~76% of AI spend on ~38% of calls - route by task class, not habit. 'The tier is the bill, not the prompt.'
2. Trend, not total. 'A 30-day total is not a run rate' - AED 211/30d hid AED 890/mo accelerating. Alert on daily/weekly run-rate slope, not a cumulative number.
3. Security. A spend spike with no matching business volume is an incident: a prompt-injection loop, an agent stuck retrying, a leaked key being abused, or a cache prefix that silently drifted ('constant length is not constant bytes' - the byte-stable prefix drifted 4x in 45 calls, destroying cache hits and doubling cost). Wire a cost-anomaly page: spend/inquiry or spend/agent-run outside a band -> alert_founder.
Coverage matters: 37 hand-rolled fetches once bypassed ai_cost_log, leaving a third of spend unmeasured. If a call path isn't routed through ai_gateway, its cost is invisible - route everything through the gateway.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/{ai_gateway,cost_snapshot}, and MEMORY 'the tier is the bill', 'a 30-day total is not a run rate', 'constant length is not constant bytes', 'the AI gateway caps output at ~900 tokens'.

title: Edge-function reliability patterns for Deno workers
content:
Supabase edge functions run on a Deno worker with a hard resource/time budget. The recurring outage class is HTTP 546 WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT - the worker exceeded memory or ~wall-time (~100s+). Patterns proven here:
1. Add invocations, never batch size. Any job whose work scales with the estate (backup, dr_drill, kb_embed) must stream/page and be RESUMABLE at fine granularity, carrying its resume cursor across HTTP hops, with a MAX_HOPS ceiling so a runaway chain stops visibly rather than looping forever. If one unit (one table, one large page) already exceeds the budget, the resume point must be smaller than that unit.
2. Fail CLOSED on auth. Secret-gated functions (verify_jwt=false) must reject empty/missing secrets, not just wrong ones. The classic bug: `if (body.__secret !== undefined && body.__secret !== expected) 403` let a bare `{}` skip the check entirely - on write endpoints that meant anonymous service-role writes. Use requireInternal(admin, body.__secret, name) which returns 503 when the verifier can't answer for ANY reason.
3. Read finish_reason before trusting output. The AI gateway caps output at ~900 tokens and `max` is often ignored; a reply cut at max_tokens arrives as ordinary content. Check choices[0].finish_reason ('length' vs 'stop') before blaming the model - this misdiagnosis has cost multiple investigations.
4. Never let logging break the function - wrap the agent_runs insert in try/catch. Error and empty must not return the same value (a catch returning [] once made an unreachable registry look populated).

title: Incident response and runbooks for a one-human-on-call company
content:
os_incidents is the incident-capture + runbook library surface. 'Get help' opens an incident (fn_os_incident_open) and notifies the founder. os_health is the read-only system-health board: failing crons, agent errors, health-check fails, and a money reconciliation, all in plain language. Together they are the operator console for a company whose only human is the founder.
The on-call model differs from a normal team: the FIRST responder is the platform (self-healing crons, retries, circuit breakers), and the human is the LAST resort, reached only through the actionability gate. So the runbook's job is to make the rare page self-service: each alert links to quotesdone.com/os and each incident type should carry a stored runbook (symptom -> the 2-3 commands or the one OS button that resolves it). Founder rule: do NOT ask him technical questions - a runbook that ends in 'ask the founder which config to use' has failed; derive and decide, page only with a decision that is genuinely his (a refund, a spend release, a boundary).
Triage order for any 'platform is misbehaving' page: (1) fn_cron_liveness - is the scheduler even alive; (2) agent_runs last 24h by agent+status - what's erroring and its note; (3) Supabase logs + get_advisors for the failing function; (4) os_health money reconciliation if anything touched payments. Recover silently, alert on the transition, and write the fix back into the runbook so the next occurrence is one click.
source: Grounded in supabase/functions/{os_incidents,os_health}/index.ts and MEMORY 'do not ask him technical questions', 'decide do not present options', 'the OS dashboard is still basic'.

title: Money reconciliation as a correctness SLO
content:
Availability is not enough for a platform that takes money - correctness is its own SLO. os_health runs a money reconciliation across three independent ledgers: internal payments (transactions), Stripe events (stripe_webhook -> stored events), and the GL balance the bookkeeper agent maintains. Any divergence is a correctness incident even when every edge function returns 200 and every cron is green.
Why three sources: a single source can be self-consistently wrong. transactions can record a charge the webhook never confirmed (optimistic write), a Stripe event can arrive for a charge the platform lost, and the GL can drift if reveal-fee revenue or supplier commissions are booked on the wrong event. The revenue model is specific: recognise reveal-fee revenue AT REVEAL; record supplier commissions as receivable at reveal and clear on collection within 14 working days; treat refunds as contra-revenue. Reconciliation must check those recognitions, not just totals.
Operational rules: (1) the webhook is the source of truth for 'did money move' - an audit row proves receipt, not success ('os_api logs before it acts'), so confirm the effect, not the log line. (2) Every refund needs the founder (his ruling: any amount, even AED 10) AND an externally issued Stripe refund is a FACT not a request - three Stripe originators are exempt from the refunds guard. (3) A non-zero reconciliation delta pages at 'critical' - money mismatches are never a soft alert.

title: Error budgets and the autonomous-company on-call model
content:
Translate 'the platform is healthy essentially all the time' into an operating rhythm, not a slogan. Each SLO (funnel availability, payment success, agent-run success, notification delivery) gets a monthly error budget; the daily conductor (fn_day_conductor / the one operating rhythm) and the weekly cost_snapshot are the review cadence. When a budget is being burned fast, the response is mechanical: freeze non-essential deploys (the read-back + change-request gates already make deploys deliberate), and route engineering effort to the burning SLI.
The on-call escalation ladder is inverted from a staffed team - automation is L1, the founder is L2 and final:
- L1 automation: retries, circuit breakers (open-circuit routes fail closed), self-healing crons, deduped health monitors (ai_health, uptime_check). These recover silently and log to agent_runs/founder_alerts at info.
- L2 human: reached only through alert_founder's actionability gate, WhatsApp for critical/urgent, always with a decision to make (not a question to answer).
- L0 external watchdog: resilience_ping guarantees the ladder itself can page even when pg_cron/pg_net are down.
Two standing rules that keep the numbers honest: 'never state what you have not measured' - a narrow green check never licenses a broad 'all healthy' claim; and a rate over zero events is not a measurement - until real marketplace volume exists, SLOs are driven by synthetic probes and the §8 harness, and that limitation is stated, not hidden.
kw: never state what you have not measured

title: Build-mode OPEN DOOR — the whole os_* operator console can run with NO JWT
content: The 7 os_* edge functions (os_ops, os_health, os_settings, os_incidents, os_automation, os_catalog, os_pages) share a build-mode "open door". Each checks the DB flag fn_os_open_access() near the top: when it returns TRUE and the request has no/invalid token, the function sets viaBuildMode, adopts identity build-mode@quotesdone.local, SKIPS admin.auth.getUser AND the app_secrets.admin_emails check, and performs real work (pause/resume/reschedule/run pg_cron jobs, catalog and settings mutations). Access is authorised by a DB flag, not by a JWT. The OS frontend (src/lib/osClient.ts) is written to send TOKENLESS requests (no Authorization header) when no session exists, precisely to use this door for operator/build-time recovery (the "session expired" case). CURRENT STATE (2 Sep 2026): the door is CLOSED — fn_os_open_access() returns false; newest public.os_open_access_log row id=3 state=closed since 2026-08-16 — so the only live traffic is the logged-in admin sending a valid Supabase JWT, and no cron/server-to-server caller exists. SECURITY IMPLICATIONS: (1) This is a deliberate, re-openable backdoor. Whoever can INSERT a state=open row into public.os_open_access_log re-opens unauthenticated admin access to the entire OS console — so write-authority on os_open_access_log IS the real control; audit who can write it and alert on any new state=open row. (2) It is exactly why the os_* functions are verify_jwt=false at the edge: verify_jwt=true would reject tokenless requests BEFORE the function runs, permanently severing the door (re-opening the flag would silently have no effect). (3) To edge-gate os_* (defense-in-depth) you must FIRST retire build mode (remove the fn_os_open_access branch + stop osClient sending tokenless requests) — a launch-time decision.
